Saint Augustine Church, New Orleans, seen from Governor Nicholls Street, 1885. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

Engraving by Henry Richard S. Bunnett (1845–1910), reconstructing Le Compain’s Hôtel at Place d’Armes and Petite rue Saint-Jacques in Old Montreal, c. 1850. Philippe Du Berger, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Hand-colored lithograph by J. C. Wild, c. 1840, showing the first St. Louis Cathedral and Bishop’s House from the southeast, with part of the church orphan asylum visible in the background. Missouri History Museum; public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

“View of the Fort of the Natchez,” by Georges Henri Victor Collot, from Voyage dans l'Amérique Septentrionale, ou Description des pays arrosés par le Mississipi, l'Ohio, le Missouri, originally published in 1796. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

2002 photo of Cherokee Plantation (1839), a French Creole architectural example, likely constructed by Charles Emile Sompeyrac after his 1837 marriage to Clarisse Prudhomme, on Highway 494 in Natchez, Natchitoches Parish, LA.
A view of reconstructed French Fort Condé and the Mobile, Alabama skyline.
Photograph from 1880 of Ste. Anne's church, built 1818, on the corner of Larned St and Bates St in downtown Detroit. The original parish was founded in 1701 (Archdiocese of Detroit Archives).

1980s photograph of a room restored to its original appearance in the Bolduc House, constructed in 1740 by prominent merchant Peter Bolduc in Ste. Geneviève, Missouri. The entire village, including this house, was relocated to higher ground in 1785 to avoid Mississippi River flooding.

Interior view of St. Francis Xavier Cathedral in Vincennes, Indiana, constructed between 1826 and 1837, looking toward the altar. Photograph taken in March 1934 as part of the Historic American Buildings Survey. Public domain image via Wikimedia Commons.

The Archambault House in Florissant, Missouri, built c. 1850 for Auguste Archambault, a French-Canadian fur trader, mountain guide, and western explorer. The house is a transitional Federal-style residence and a contributing property in the St. Ferdinand Central Historic District. Via Wikimedia Commons.
View of New Madrid, Missouri, from Henry Lewis’s Das illustrirte Mississippithal, published in Düsseldorf in 1857. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons and Internet Archive Book Images.
Melrose Plantation’s Big House in Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana, part of the Cane River Creole landscape. Historic American Buildings Survey photograph. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.
View of Kaskaskia, Illinois, published in Meyer’s Universum, vol. 18 (1857). Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

Plan of Cape Girardeau, Missouri, based on Georges-Henri-Victor Collot’s 1796 survey of the Mississippi Valley and published in 1826. The map shows the settlement, surrounding landscape, and a nearby Shawnee camp. Public domain, Library of Congress.
Church of the Holy Family, Cahokia, Illinois, built in 1799 in the French colonial poteaux-sur-sol tradition. Historic American Buildings Survey photograph. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.
Fort Crèvecœur, near present-day Peoria, Illinois, as depicted in a 1932 Illinois Historical Society publication. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

Bombardment and Capture of Fort Hindman, Arkansas Post, January 11, 1863. Lithograph by Currier & Ives, hand-colored. No known publication restrictions. Courtesy of the Library of Congress via Wikimedia Commons.

Aerial view of reconstructed Fort Michilimackinac at Mackinaw City, Michigan, site of the French fort and trading community established in 1715. Photograph by WMrapids, 2022. CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.
French (Creole) House, Prairie du Rocher, Illinois. Photograph by Clark Bullard, April 1935. Historic American Buildings Survey, Library of Congress.
Historic François Vertefeuille House near Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin. Photograph by Jonathunder, July 12, 2009. CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Étienne and Louise LaMarque House, Old Mines, Missouri, built in 1818 and acquired by the LaMarque family in 1822. The house is an example of the French colonial architectural tradition that survived in the Old Mines community. Via Wikimedia Commons.

Fort Harrison on the Wabash River near present-day Terre Haute, Indiana, depicted as it appeared in 1812. Lithograph by James A. Modesitt and Luther G. Hager, 1848. Library of Congress; no known restrictions on publication.
U.S. postage stamp issued for Wisconsin’s 1934 tercentenary, depicting Jean Nicolet’s arrival at Green Bay in 1634. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

Manuscript map of Fort Wayne, Indiana, July 18, 1795, showing the American fort across the St. Marys River from the Miami village of Kekionga and the remains of old Fort Miami. Drawn by P. M. Neff for General Anthony Wayne. Library of Congress Geography and Map Division; public domain.

Statue of Solomon Juneau in Milwaukee, photographed circa 1890. Juneau, a French Canadian fur trader, settled permanently at Milwaukee in 1818 and became the city’s first mayor. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

Portage des Sioux Common Field, Missouri, shown in a 1905 plat preserving the long, narrow lots characteristic of the French colonial common-field system. Library of Congress Geography and Map Division. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

Grand Rapids, Michigan, in 1831, showing the Baptist mission west of the Grand River and Louis Campau’s trading post at center right. Campau, a French Canadian fur trader, established the post in 1826. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

Pierre Navarre Cabin, South Bend, Indiana. Navarre, a French fur trader, established a trading post on the St. Joseph River in 1820 and lived here with his Potawatomi wife, Keshewaquay (Angelique), and their family. Via Wikimedia Commons.

Julien Dubuque Monument at the Mines of Spain, overlooking the Mississippi River south of Dubuque, Iowa. The monument, erected in 1897, marks Dubuque’s burial site within the lead-mining landscape associated with his late eighteenth-century settlement. Photograph by Harry N. Bevers, 1934. Historic American Buildings Survey, Library of Congress; public domain.

Site of Fort St. Joseph near Niles, Michigan, a French mission, garrison, and trading post established in the late seventeenth century on the St. Joseph River. Photograph by Chris Light, 2010. CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Confluence of the Eel River (French Rivière à l’Anguille) and Wabash River at Logansport, Indiana, circa 1905–1907. Postcard published by the Souvenir Post Card Co. Amon Carter Museum of American Art; public domain.

Antoine LeClaire House, Davenport, Iowa, built in 1855. LeClaire, the son of a French Canadian father and Potawatomi mother, was an interpreter and landowner whose property formed the basis of the town of Davenport. Via Wikimedia Commons.

Shawnee man from the Apple Creek (Rivière à la Pomme) community, drawn by Joseph Warin during Victor Collot’s 1796 journey through the Mississippi Valley and published in 1826. Under Spanish rule, Shawnee and Delaware migrants established several large villages along Apple Creek, including Le Grand Village Sauvage and Petit Village Sauvage. Their communities were closely connected to the region’s French-speaking population, and some houses were built in French colonial style with closely set vertical posts, clay infill, and shingled roofs. Library of Congress Geography and Map Division; public domain.

Historical marker at Fort Ouiatenon near West Lafayette, Indiana. The French established the fort on the Wabash River in 1717 as a trading post and diplomatic center. Photograph taken January 28, 2007. Public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

Fountain Cave on the Mississippi River near St. Paul, Minnesota, photographed by Whitney & Zimmerman, circa 1859–1890. French Canadian trader Pierre “Pig’s Eye” Parrant established a tavern near the cave in 1838, part of the early river settlement from which St. Paul developed. New York Public Library; public domain via Wikimedia Commons.

Powder magazine at Fort de Chartres, near Prairie du Rocher, Illinois, part of the eighteenth-century French stone fort. Photograph by Lester Jones, October 1, 1940. Historic American Buildings Survey, Library of Congress; no known restrictions on publication.
